description: Flame in Freefall is an AI-powered scientific intelligence platform that analyses NASA's microgravity combustion datasets to understand how flames behave in space. Using machine learning, data analytics, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), it identifies combustion patterns, compares experiments, and generates evidence-based fire-safety insights. The goal is to support safer spacecraft design and improve fire prevention strategies for future Moon and Mars missions.
summary: Flame in Freefall is an AI-powered dashboard that turns NASA's microgravity combustion research into actionable spacecraft fire-safety intelligence. Long-duration spaceflight removes buoyant convection the force that makes flames rise, cool, and self-limit on Earth, so materials that are safe in a 1g lab can sustain combustion at oxygen levels that would self-extinguish terrestrially. We parsed NASA Technical Reports Server documents from the BASS, BASS-II, and Confined Combustion programs into 51 structured test conditions covering 13 materials, computed a composite Fire Risk Index (flammability + persistence), and built an interactive dashboard with a ranked risk table, a side-by-side experiment comparison tool, and a retrieval-augmented AI research assistant that answers questions in plain language, grounded only in indexed NASA reports with inline citations back to the source NTRS record. Every number on the dashboard traces back to a real NASA document.
details:
Flame in Freefall ingests real NASA technical reports (PDF), extracts them into structured test-condition records (material, oxygen %, flow velocity, outcome), computes a composite Fire Risk Index for each material, and indexes the same reports into a local vector store for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

How it works: NTRS report PDFs -> text extraction -> structured CSV (51 test conditions, 13 materials) -> Fire Risk Index = 0.6 x flammability_norm + 0.4 x persistence_norm, normalized across the dataset -> ChromaDB vector index queried by a locally-run LLM for the AI research assistant.

The dashboard has four views: an Overview with ranked fire-safety vulnerability and hero metrics; an Experiment Browser to filter all 51 real test runs by material, oxygen concentration, and platform; a Comparison tool for side-by-side multi-run analysis; and an AI Research Assistant that answers natural-language questions and cites the exact NASA document and NTRS link behind every claim, so it never answers from outside the indexed reports.

Tools/languages: Next.js 16 (React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS) for the frontend; FastAPI (Python) for the backend; pandas for data processing; ChromaDB for the vector store; Ollama running llama3.1:8b (chat) and nomic-embed-text (embeddings) for a fully local, open-source RAG pipeline with no external API dependency.

Impact: mission planners and materials engineers can identify high fire-risk spacecraft interior materials without manually reading dozens of NASA technical reports, and can ask the assistant direct questions grounded in that literature instead of guessing.

AI assistance disclosure: Claude (Anthropic) was used throughout development as a coding and writing assistant for backend/frontend implementation, the NASA report data-extraction pipeline, UI/UX design iteration, and drafting on-site copy (landing page content, this submission text). No NASA logos, flags, or mission identifiers were used or modified; the hero photograph is an unmodified public-domain NASA image, credited in-page. All data figures and citations were verified against the source NASA Technical Reports Server documents, not generated by SI.
